weeks.title: Character and Inner Alignment
weeks.description: This week, we begin by discussing alignment through the perspective of instilling “good character” in models. We start with Emergent Misalignment, which demonstrates that models trained on harmful code completions generalize to broadly misaligned behavior on unrelated tasks. To help explain this surprising result, we turn to Anthropic’s Persona Selection Model, which proposes a mental model of LLMs as actors capable of simulating a vast repertoire of characters. From this perspective, a relatively small amount of flawed training can push models away from the Assistant persona and towards problematic personas. We then examine Alignment Faking, which shows that models may strategically comply with its training objective to prevent its existing preferences from being changed. We end with mesa-optimization and inner alignment, examining how a model can learn to pursue an objective that produces the desired training behavior but undesirable deployment behavior. The goal of this week is to conclude our discussion of (mis)alignment with a broad picture of how training shapes an LLM’s character and how this process can produce behavior we didn’t intend.

articles.title: Recent Developments in AI
articles.html:
Anthropic pledges 5% of its shares to a public benefit fund

On October 18, Anthropic announced plans to commit 5% of Anthropic shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, subject to stockholder approval. An additional 2% is proposed to be added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline. None of the Anthropic equity will be used for lobbying or political giving.

Anthropic’s seven co-founders have already pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings to philanthropic and public-interest causes and have established an aggressive donor matching program for employees, which around half of employees participate in. Anthropic says these commitments, including the proposed fund allocation, would together dedicate roughly 20% of its shares to the public good. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a November 2026 IPO with a valuation expectation around $2 trillion.

OpenAI’s nonprofit Foundation similarly funds philanthropic work. It also has a distinct governance role: controlling OpenAI’s commercial business, OpenAI Group PBC. At the October 2025 restructuring, the Foundation held 26% of its shares, Microsoft 27%, and employees and other investors 47%. Despite its minority stake, the Foundation retains the right to appoint and replace OpenAI Group’s entire board.

Sources: Anthropic announcement (October 18); OpenAI’s structure; Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust; Redfin; TechCrunch; Cinco Días (October 20).

AI money in the 2026 midterms

The 2026 elections have featured heavy spending from the AI industry. The “pro-innovation” side has been led by Leading the Future, a network of super PACs whose largest backers include venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, OpenAI president Greg Brockman, and his wife Anna Brockman. Leading the Future has a mission to “ensure AI leadership remains a central focus in U.S. politics” and has backed candidates who favor light-touch national regulations. The “pro-safety” side has been led by Public First Action, a 501(c)4 nonprofit that supports AI safety, transparency, and oversight. Public First Action’s largest known donor is Anthropic.

As of October 20, Transformer News reported that $66.84 million have been spent by AI-focused super PACs so far on 2026 elections. $31.57 million came from “pro-innovation” groups, and $35.27 million came from “pro-safety” groups. Both sides have contributed to both Democrats and Republicans.

Sources: Transformer’s FEC tracker (October 20); tracker methodology; New York Times (September 30); OpenAI statement (June 1).
